notes.title: What justifies a second agent

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The two justifications that held up in production, and the token multiple they cost — How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

  • Start simple; add agents only when a single one provably can't do it — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Single-agent vs Multi-agent — the comparison and what multi-agent systems are.

  • When Multi-Agent Hurts — the cases where it actively costs you.

  • Role Specialization — roles as a design device, and their limits.

What this note adds: the two justifications that survive scrutiny, the arithmetic to bring to the argument, and the rehearsed answer for the interviewer who wants five specialist agents because the org chart has five teams.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The only two justifications? Genuinely parallel work, or contexts that would poison each other.
The one that isn't? "Roles look tidy." Specialisation is a prompt, not a process.
The number to quote? ~15× chat tokens for multi-agent; ~4× for a single agent.
What compounds across handoffs? Errors — and context that silently didn't survive the boundary.
The cheaper alternative to try first? One agent with better tools, or sub-agents for context only.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I justify a second agent on exactly two grounds: the work splits into parts that genuinely run in parallel, or a subtask needs a large context that would poison the main one. That's it. "A researcher agent and a writer agent and an editor agent" is role-play — specialisation is a prompt, and I can change the prompt between steps of one agent for free. The reason to be strict is the price: Anthropic's published figures put multi-agent at roughly fifteen times chat tokens, and errors compound across every handoff. If I can't name which of the two justifications applies, the answer is one agent.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
One agent The work is sequential and fits one context. The default. Long runs accumulate context and rot; no parallelism. A single line of reasoning from start to finish.
One agent + sub-agents for context A subtask generates a lot of material the main line doesn't need. Token multiplication on that branch; a summary at the boundary. One stage drowns the window.
Orchestrator + parallel workers Subtasks are genuinely independent and run at the same time. ~15× tokens; coordination failures; errors compound. "For each of these N things, do the same work."
Peer agents / handoff Distinct systems with separate owners, tools or trust domains. Everything above, plus an interop contract between teams. The agents belong to different teams or products.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
One agent Loop, tools, one context. ~4× chat tokens. Cost grows with steps². One trace to read. Failures name a step.
Sub-agents for context A child agent with its own window and a return contract. Adds the child's full run; the parent pays only for the summary. Handoff loss is the new failure: what the summary dropped.
Orchestrator + workers Orchestrator, delegation contract, worker pool, result merge. ~15× chat tokens. Latency is the slowest worker, not the average. Duplicated work, conflicting writes, workers that never finish.
Peer agents An interop protocol and a trust boundary between agents. Same as above plus protocol overhead. Cross-team on-call; version skew between agents.

The redraw test: every option past the first adds agent boxes and a merge point. If your diagram has three agents and no merge node, nobody has decided what happens when two of them disagree.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The multiple that settles most arguments. Anthropic's research-system write-up reports that agents use roughly 4× the tokens of a chat interaction and multi-agent systems roughly 15×. That is the sentence to have ready, because "multi-agent is expensive" is an opinion and "fifteen times" is a budget conversation.

Where the multiple comes from. Each agent maintains its own context and re-bills it per step, so you're not paying for N agents — you're paying for N independent steps² curves, plus the orchestrator's own reasoning about delegation and merging. Parallelism buys wall-clock, never tokens.

Error compounding across handoffs. If each agent succeeds with probability p and there are k handoffs, end-to-end success is bounded by roughly p^(k+1) — before counting the coordination failures that only exist because there are multiple agents. At p = 0.9 with three workers and a merge, that's 0.9^4 ≈ 0.66. The same work in one agent is a single p, which is why "split it up to make it more reliable" usually has the sign backwards.

The test to run before splitting. Take the tasks you believe are parallel and check whether any worker's input depends on another's output. If one does, they aren't parallel — they're a sequence, and sequencing them across agents adds handoffs without adding concurrency, which is the worst cell in the table.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["📋 The task"] --> B{"🔀 Do parts run at<br/>the same time?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C{"🔀 Are they truly<br/>independent?"}
    B -->|"no"| D{"🔀 Does one subtask flood<br/>the context window?"}
    C -->|"yes"| E(["👥 Orchestrator + parallel workers"])
    C -->|"no — one feeds another"| F(["1️⃣ One agent, sequential"])
    D -->|"yes"| G(["🧩 One agent + sub-agent for context"])
    D -->|"no"| F

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

Notice what isn't on the diagram: roles, expertise, and org structure. None of them reach a terminal node, because none of them is a reason to pay the multiple. If the only argument for splitting is that the parts have different names, the answer is one agent with different prompts per step.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We built five specialist agents and it's slower, more expensive, and worse than the single agent it replaced."

Root cause. The split followed the team's mental model of the work — a researcher, an analyst, a writer, a fact-checker, an editor — rather than any property of the task. The five stages were strictly sequential, so nothing ran in parallel and the only thing gained was four handoffs. Each handoff passed a summary, and detail that mattered downstream kept not surviving: the fact-checker couldn't verify claims because the sources hadn't been carried forward, so it verified what it could and passed the rest through. Cost went up roughly as expected; quality went down because p^5 beat the improvement from specialisation.

Fix. One agent with a staged prompt — the same five stages as instructions rather than as processes — and sub-agents retained only for parallel source gathering, which was the one genuinely concurrent part. The lesson that generalises: a pipeline of roles is a workflow, and running a workflow across agents buys handoffs rather than concurrency.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Specialisation improves quality though — a focused prompt beats a general one. Isn't that a justification?

Focused prompts do help, and that's an argument for changing the prompt between steps, not for spawning a process. One agent can carry a different instruction at each stage of its own loop, which gets the specialisation benefit at zero coordination cost.

What a separate agent adds beyond the prompt is an isolated context and an independent execution. If I don't need either of those, I'm paying for process boundaries to get a benefit that lives in the text.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When does context isolation alone justify a sub-agent, given the token multiple?

When a subtask would otherwise dominate the parent's window and the parent doesn't need the detail — searching fifty documents to answer one question, or reading a large codebase to make one decision. The sub-agent burns its own context and returns a summary, so the parent stays coherent for the rest of a long run.

The trade is that you're paying the child's full run to save the parent's accumulation. That's worth it when the parent is long-lived, because parent context is re-billed every subsequent step, and it's not worth it when the parent is about to finish anyway.

The failure to watch is the summary. If the parent routinely needs something the child dropped, you've bought context isolation and paid for it in handoff loss.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Ten parallel workers. What breaks first?

The merge, not the workers. Ten independent results have to be reconciled, and the orchestrator reads all of them — so the parent's context grows with worker count, which is the thing parallelism was supposed to avoid. Past a handful of workers the orchestrator becomes the bottleneck and the context-rot problem relocates rather than disappearing.

The shape that scales is hierarchical: workers return structured summaries rather than raw findings, and an intermediate layer reconciles groups before the top-level merge. The other thing that breaks is provider rate limits — ten concurrent workers multiply your token-per-minute usage, and hitting the limit turns parallelism back into a queue, often without anyone noticing that the concurrency stopped being real.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design a system where sub-agent count adapts to the work rather than being fixed.

I'd have the orchestrator plan the decomposition and emit a worker count as an output of planning, bounded by a hard cap the orchestrator can't exceed. The cap matters because decomposition is exactly where a model over-produces — asked to split work, it will happily find twelve subtasks in something with three.

Each worker gets an explicit delegation contract: objective, output schema, tool subset, and an effort budget in steps. The budget is per worker and the sum is checked against the run's total, so the orchestrator is spending from a fixed pool rather than allocating freely. That turns "how many workers" into a resource-allocation decision with a visible constraint.

What I'd measure is marginal value per worker — task success and cost as worker count varies on the same inputs. In practice there's a knee, and finding it empirically is far more useful than reasoning about it, because it depends on how genuinely separable the corpus is.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Multi-agent systems are more reliable — each agent is simpler, so each is more accurate."

✅ Reality: Per-agent accuracy rises and end-to-end success falls, because handoffs multiply. Three workers plus a merge at p = 0.9 is roughly 0.66. Simpler components don't help when you've added terms to the exponent.

❌ Trap: "Split by role — researcher, writer, reviewer — it mirrors how a team works."

✅ Reality: A team works that way because people can't share a context window. Agents can. Role decomposition without parallelism or context pressure buys handoffs and nothing else, and it's the single most common wrong answer in this round.

❌ Trap: "Parallel agents make it faster, so the cost is justified by latency."

✅ Reality: Parallelism buys wall-clock and costs tokens — roughly 15× against chat. That's a fine trade when latency is the binding constraint, and an expensive one when it isn't. Say which constraint you're spending against.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Single-agent vs Multi-agent — the comparison this note decides.

  • When Multi-Agent Hurts — the standing case against.

  • the 95% problem — the compounding behind the handoff arithmetic.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Which rung of the ladder — this is that ladder's fourth rung, examined properly.

  • §6 Orchestrator-worker — the shape you get once this says yes.

  • §5 Context rot — sub-agent isolation is the context-driven reason to split.

  • §10 Cost modeling — the 15× is where a multi-agent budget starts.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — parallel source gathering is the justification that genuinely holds.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — almost never multi-agent, and saying why is the point.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Detailed task descriptions for sub-agents, and the effort-scaling rule — How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

  • Handoffs as a first-class primitive with an explicit input contract — OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Orchestrator-Worker Pattern — the pattern and why it's the production default.

  • Manager Sub-agent Delegation — how delegation is wired.

What this note adds: the contract's four fields and what each one prevents. The pattern notes say delegate; this says what an under-specified delegation costs — duplicated work, sub-agents that never finish, and results that can't be merged.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four fields? Objective · output format · tool subset · effort budget.
What a missing objective causes? Overlap — two workers choosing the same obvious subtask.
What a missing output format causes? A merge step that has to parse prose.
What a missing effort budget causes? Workers that never finish, or over-invest in an easy subtask.
Who decides the split? The orchestrator, before dispatch. Never the workers, concurrently.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

A delegation is a contract with four fields, and each one exists because omitting it produces a specific failure. The objective has to be specific enough that two workers can't pick the same subtask — vague briefs cause overlap. The output format has to be a schema, or the merge step is parsing prose. The tool subset scopes what the worker can reach. And the effort budget — a step or token cap proportional to the subtask's difficulty — is what stops a worker spending the run's budget on the easiest part. Under-specified delegation is the single most common cause of multi-agent systems costing more and delivering less.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Full contract — objective, format, tools, budget Anything with parallel workers. The default. Orchestrator must plan properly before dispatching. Workers return mergeable results and finish on time.
Objective only Prototype, or one worker at a time. Overlap, unbounded effort, and a merge that parses text. "Go research X" with no shape to the answer.
Contract + explicit non-goals Workers keep straying into each other's territory. More planning tokens per dispatch. Overlap persists even with distinct objectives.
Worker self-selects from a queue Many small homogeneous subtasks. Needs atomic claim semantics, or you're back to overlap. A work queue, not a decomposition.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Full contract The orchestrator plans and allocates before any worker starts. Budgets sum to a known ceiling — the run's cost becomes bounded. Per-worker budget consumption is a live metric.
Objective only Dispatch without allocation. Unbounded per worker; total is whatever they spend. Stuck workers need a watchdog you'll have to add later.
With non-goals Objectives carry exclusions as well as inclusions. Slightly more planning tokens; far less duplicated work. Overlap rate drops and becomes measurable.
Self-select A claimable queue with atomic assignment. Efficient — no worker idles. Claim races become the failure; needs real locking.

The redraw test: a full contract makes the orchestrator's planning step a visible node with an allocation output. If workers appear in the diagram with an unlabelled arrow from the orchestrator, the contract doesn't exist yet.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Effort budgets as the cost ceiling. With N workers each capped at S steps, the run's worker cost is bounded by N × S steps plus the orchestrator's own. Without the cap, a single worker that decides its subtask is interesting can consume more than the other N-1 combined — and because it looks like productive work in the trace, nothing flags it. Anthropic's guidance is explicit that effort should scale with task complexity, which means the budget is part of the decomposition rather than a global default.

Overlap as a measurable quantity. After a run, compare what workers actually touched — sources fetched, records read. Overlap above a small fraction means the objectives weren't disjoint, and the fix is in the orchestrator's planning prompt, not in the workers. It's worth measuring because overlap is invisible in the output: two workers finding the same document produces a confident, well-supported, redundant answer.

Why the output schema pays for itself. A typed return lets the merge be code — dedupe by source id, concatenate by field, detect contradictions on the same attribute. A prose return forces the merge to be another model call reading N documents, which costs tokens, adds a failure mode, and re-introduces the context problem parallelism was meant to solve.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["🧠 Orchestrator has a plan"] --> B["1️⃣ Objective — specific enough<br/>to be exclusive"]
    B --> C["2️⃣ Output format — a schema<br/>the merge can consume"]
    C --> D["3️⃣ Tool subset — only what<br/>this subtask needs"]
    D --> E["4️⃣ Effort budget — steps,<br/>scaled to difficulty"]
    E --> F{"🔀 Could two workers<br/>read this the same way?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G(["➕ Add explicit non-goals"])
    F -->|"no"| H(["🚀 Dispatch"])
    G --> H

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The check at the end is the one worth running out loud: read each objective as a worker would and ask whether the most obvious interpretation collides with another's. If it might, name the exclusion explicitly — "cover the regulatory angle, not the technical one, which another worker has".

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "One sub-agent ran for twenty minutes on a trivial sub-question while the others finished in two."

Root cause. The orchestrator dispatched four workers with objectives and nothing else. Three subtasks were narrow and finished quickly. The fourth — "investigate the competitive landscape" — was open-ended, and the worker had no budget and no definition of enough, so it kept finding adjacent things worth checking. Each step looked productive in isolation. It stopped only when the global wall-clock timeout fired, by which point it had consumed most of the run's token budget and returned an unstructured wall of text the merge couldn't use.

Fix. Effort budgets scaled to subtask difficulty, a required output schema, and a rule in the orchestrator's planning prompt that any objective it can't bound should be decomposed further before dispatch. The broader point is that "how much effort is this worth" is the orchestrator's job — a worker has no way to know what the rest of the run is doing.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why does the orchestrator allocate the budget rather than letting workers use what they need?

Because a worker sees one subtask and can't tell whether it's the important one. The orchestrator has the decomposition, so it's the only component that knows this subtask is one of four and worth a quarter of the budget.

It's the same reason you'd size a thread pool centrally rather than letting each task decide its own priority. Local optimisation without global information produces exactly the twenty-minute worker in the failure story.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A rigid output schema constrains what a worker can report. Doesn't that lose nuance?

It does, and that's mostly the point — the merge has to consume it. What I'd do is make the schema carry a structured core plus one free-text field for anything that didn't fit, so nuance has a home without the merge having to parse it.

The field to watch is that free-text one. If workers routinely put load-bearing findings there, the schema is missing something and the fix is to extend it, not to loosen it. That's a signal you get for free and only because the schema exists.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

A worker fails or times out. What does the orchestrator do, and how does that change with twenty workers?

At small counts I'd retry once with the same contract and then proceed with a partial result, flagging the gap in the final output — a report that says which angle wasn't covered is more useful than one that quietly omits it.

At twenty workers, partial failure stops being exceptional and becomes the normal case: if each worker succeeds 95% of the time, the chance all twenty succeed is about 36%. So the merge has to be designed for incompleteness from the start rather than treating it as an error, and the orchestrator needs a notion of which subtasks are load-bearing versus supplementary. That distinction belongs in the contract too — a criticality flag, so the orchestrator knows whether to retry hard or move on.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design delegation for a system where workers are agents owned by other teams.

The contract becomes a published interface rather than a prompt, because the other team ships changes without telling me. So: a typed request and response schema, a declared effort budget the worker is obliged to respect, and a declared tool scope — with the orchestrator enforcing the budget externally rather than trusting the worker to honour it.

Trust is the part that changes most. An in-house sub-agent's output can be merged directly; another team's agent is an untrusted source, so its results need the same validation as any external input, including the assumption that its text might carry injected instructions. That argues for structured-only returns across team boundaries, with free text treated as data rather than as anything the orchestrator reasons over directly.

Versioning then matters more than anything else. I'd want the contract versioned with a compatibility policy, and integration tests that run the real worker rather than a mock — because the failure mode is a semantic change to what "covered the regulatory angle" means, which no schema check catches.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Give the sub-agent the full context so it has everything it needs."

✅ Reality: That defeats the purpose. Context isolation is one of the only two justifications for a sub-agent, so passing the parent's window through spends the token multiple and keeps the rot. Pass the objective and let it gather its own.

❌ Trap: "Workers can coordinate between themselves to avoid overlap."

✅ Reality: Coordination through shared state between non-deterministic parallel readers is a race — they all read before any writes. Disjointness is the orchestrator's job, decided once before dispatch.

❌ Trap: "Effort budgets are premature optimisation — let's see what it costs first."

✅ Reality: Unbounded workers don't reveal the natural cost; they reveal the timeout. The first uncapped run tells you what your wall-clock limit is, not what the task needs, and you'll have paid full price to learn it.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Manager Sub-agent Delegation — the delegation mechanism.

  • Coordination Problems — the failures each contract field prevents.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §6 Single vs multi-agent — the contract is what you owe once that says yes.

  • §8 Hard budgets — per-worker effort budgets are that section applied to delegation.

  • §5 Shared state across agents — a good contract removes most of the need for shared state.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — the lead-and-searchers contract is the whole design.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — cross-team delegation is the Tier 4 answer.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The 4× and 15× token figures, and the tasks that justified them — How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

  • Consistency across runs as the reliability metric, which is what handoffs erode — Measuring agent reliability: pass^k (arXiv 2507.10995)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • cost modeling — how agent cost is modelled generally.

  • the 95% problem — compounding per-step error.

  • Coordination Problems — the failure classes unique to multi-agent.

What this note adds: the two numbers said out loud, and the case where they're worth paying. Cost modelling covers a single agent's arithmetic; this covers what changes when you multiply agents — including the part people get backwards, which is that splitting work usually lowers reliability.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two multiples? Single agent ~4× chat tokens; multi-agent ~15×.
Does parallelism save tokens? No — it buys wall-clock. Tokens go up.
What handoffs do to reliability? Add exponents: p^(k+1) before coordination failures.
When is 15× defensible? Value scales with breadth — research, wide search, coverage.
The unit to argue in? Cost per successful task, not per run.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Two numbers decide most of these conversations. A single agent runs about four times the tokens of a chat interaction, and a multi-agent system about fifteen — those are Anthropic's published figures from their research system. So the question isn't whether multi-agent is expensive, it's whether the task's value scales with breadth. Research does: more parallel searchers means more ground covered, and that's worth paying for. A support workflow doesn't — splitting it across agents adds handoffs, and handoffs add exponents to the reliability arithmetic rather than reducing them.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Pay the 15× Value scales with breadth or parallel coverage. The bill, and coordination failures as a new class. "Search widely", "cover all angles", "compare N things".
Cap the worker count Multi-agent is right but the budget isn't open-ended. Coverage stops at the cap — you must say what's uncovered. Diminishing returns visible past a few workers.
One agent, more steps Sequential work where breadth isn't the value. Longer wall-clock; context accumulation. The parts feed each other.
Hybrid — fixed workflow, agents on the tail Most cases resolve cheaply, a minority need breadth. Two paths to maintain and route between. 80% of traffic is routine.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Pay the 15× Orchestrator, workers, merge, per-worker budgets. ~15× chat tokens per run. Spend cap becomes mandatory, not advisory. Per-worker cost attribution; a runaway worker is a real incident.
Cap workers A hard N the orchestrator can't exceed. Bounded: N × S steps plus the orchestrator. Coverage gaps must be reported, not hidden.
One agent No orchestrator, no merge. ~4×. Grows with steps². One trace. Failures name a step.
Hybrid A router, a cheap path, and an expensive path. Weighted by traffic mix — usually the best cost per success. Fall-through rate is the metric that says the router is right.

The redraw test: paying the multiple means a spend cap appears in the gateway and a per-worker budget appears in the delegation. If the diagram has workers but no cap anywhere, the cost conversation hasn't happened.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The two multiples, and what they're against. Anthropic report roughly 4× chat tokens for an agent and 15× for their multi-agent research system. Both are measured against a chat interaction, so they compose with everything else — a multi-agent run that also does long context accumulation is 15× and steps².

Why splitting work usually lowers reliability. With k handoffs each at per-agent success p, end-to-end is roughly p^(k+1):

p = 0.9, one agent          → 0.90
p = 0.9, 3 workers + merge  → 0.9^4 ≈ 0.66

Then add the failures that exist only because there are multiple agents — duplicated work, conflicting writes, context lost at a handoff. This is the part that gets stated backwards most often in rounds: "we split it so each agent is simpler and more reliable" describes per-agent accuracy while the system's number falls.

The unit that makes the case honestly. Cost per successful task, not per run:

cost_per_success = cost_per_run / task_success_rate

A multi-agent run at 15× that lifts success from 55% to 85% has a real argument — the denominator moved enough to matter. A multi-agent run at 15× that leaves success flat is a 15× cost increase with a nicer diagram, and that's the comparison to insist on when someone proposes the split.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["💭 Someone proposes multi-agent"] --> B{"🔀 Does value scale<br/>with breadth?"}
    B -->|"no"| C(["1️⃣ One agent — say the 15×"])
    B -->|"yes"| D{"🔀 Is the budget<br/>open-ended?"}
    D -->|"no"| E(["🔢 Cap N; report coverage gaps"])
    D -->|"yes"| F{"🔀 Does most traffic<br/>need the breadth?"}
    F -->|"no"| G(["🔀 Hybrid — cheap path, agents on the tail"])
    F -->|"yes"| H(["👥 Pay it, with per-worker budgets"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The first branch is the whole decision. "Does value scale with breadth" is answerable from the brief, and it separates research and wide-search problems — where more coverage is more value — from transactional ones, where doing the same task with more agents just costs more.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The multi-agent version won the demo and we shut it off six weeks after launch."

Root cause. The demo compared output quality on a handful of curated questions, where breadth genuinely helped and the multi-agent answer was visibly richer. Nobody compared cost per successful task, and in production the traffic mix was different: most questions were narrow and resolved by one searcher, but every question paid for five. Success barely moved against the single-agent baseline because the marginal workers were covering ground the question didn't need, while the bill scaled with the worker count on every request.

Fix. A router — cheap single-agent path by default, multi-agent only for questions classified as broad — which recovered most of the quality at a fraction of the cost. The diagnostic that would have caught it pre-launch is the one that was skipped: measure cost per success on representative traffic, not on the questions that motivated the design.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Where do the 4× and 15× actually come from?

They're Anthropic's published figures from their research system — token usage against a chat interaction. I quote them as an order of magnitude rather than a constant, because they depend on the task, but they're the best public anchor available and they're defensible in a way "it's expensive" isn't.

The mechanism is straightforward: each agent maintains its own context and re-bills it per step, so you're paying for several independent accumulation curves plus the orchestrator reasoning about delegation and merging. That's why parallelism doesn't help the token line at all.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

If it's 15× and usually less reliable, when is it ever right?

When the value is breadth and the alternative is not covering the ground at all. A research task where five parallel searchers each explore a different angle produces something one agent sequentially cannot in the same wall-clock, and the extra coverage is the product.

The second case is context isolation — a subtask that would poison the main window. There the multiple buys coherence in a long parent run, which is a quality argument rather than a throughput one.

What both have in common is that I can name what the extra agents produce, not just what they do. If the answer is "the same output, faster", the honest framing is that I'm buying latency at 15×, and that trade should be stated as such.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At 100× traffic, what does the 15× do to your infrastructure planning?

It moves the binding constraint from compute to provider rate limits, usually well before the bill becomes the blocker. Each run now issues several concurrent model calls, so tokens-per-minute scales with runs multiplied by worker count, and you hit the account limit at a fraction of the traffic you'd expect. When that happens, workers queue — so the parallelism you're paying for stops being real while you keep paying for it.

The planning consequence is that worker count is a capacity parameter, not just a quality one. I'd want per-tenant concurrency limits so one tenant's broad queries can't starve everyone else's, priority lanes so interactive traffic isn't queued behind batch, and an explicit degradation path — reduce worker count under pressure rather than queueing, because a narrower answer now beats a broad answer after a timeout.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the cost controls for a multi-agent product where customers pay per seat.

Per-seat pricing and variable per-run cost is the mismatch to solve, so the control has to be a budget the customer can't exceed and the system enforces without failing rudely. I'd put a spend cap per tenant in the gateway — the only place outside the run — and a per-run cap that bounds worker count and per-worker steps.

Degradation matters more than enforcement. Hitting a cap should reduce breadth, not error: fewer workers, narrower objectives, an answer that says which angles weren't covered. A customer who gets a narrower answer is fine; one who gets a failure after ninety seconds is not.

For unit economics I'd track cost per successful task per tenant, because the average hides everything. A small number of tenants asking broad questions will dominate spend, and the answer is usually a product decision — a tier, or a per-run breadth control the user sets — rather than an engineering one. That's the conversation the numbers exist to enable.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Parallel agents are cheaper because they finish faster."

✅ Reality: Faster and cheaper are different axes. Parallelism reduces wall-clock and increases tokens — you pay for every branch whether or not its output mattered. If latency is the constraint, say so; it's a legitimate reason to spend.

❌ Trap: "Splitting the task across specialists makes the system more reliable."

✅ Reality: Per-agent accuracy goes up, end-to-end goes down. Each handoff adds a term: three workers plus a merge at p=0.9 is about 0.66. Reliability comes from fewer steps and real verification, not from more boundaries.

❌ Trap: "We'll measure cost per run and optimise from there."

✅ Reality: Failed runs cost money and deliver nothing, so the unit is cost per successful task. It's also the only unit where a multi-agent system can win — the whole argument is that the denominator moves enough to justify the numerator.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • cost modeling — the single-agent arithmetic this extends.

  • the 95% problem — compounding, applied across handoffs.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §6 Single vs multi-agent — this note is the number that argues it.

  • §10 Spend caps per run and per tenant — the 15× is why they stop being optional.

  • §1 Metrics before boxes — cost per successful task is the unit this argument needs.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — where the multiple is defensible, with the caps to prove it.

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — demoting an unjustified multi-agent split is often the first fix.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Handoff as a topology primitive — control transfers rather than returns — OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs

  • Supervisor and swarm architectures side by side — LangGraph: multi-agent

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Orchestration Topologies — the topologies and how each is wired.

  • Group chat round-robin — the conversational shapes and their cost profile.

What this note adds: the property that selects one. The topologies note describes them; this says that the choice is really about who holds control and whether it comes back — which is a two-question test rather than a menu.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The selecting question? Does control return to a coordinator, or transfer away?
Production default? Hierarchical supervisor — control returns, one place merges.
When handoff/swarm? Distinct domains where the next agent owns the rest of the task.
Why group chat is rarely right? Every agent reads every turn — cost grows with agents × turns.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Once multi-agent is justified, the topology question is really two questions: does control come back, and is there one place results are merged. If control returns and merging is central, that's a hierarchical supervisor, which is the production default for good reason — it's the only shape where budgets and merge logic live in one place. If control transfers permanently, that's a handoff or swarm, which suits distinct domains where the receiving agent genuinely owns the rest. Group chat and round-robin are mostly demo shapes: every agent reads every turn, so cost grows with agents times turns for coordination you could have made explicit.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Sequential pipeline Fixed stages, each consuming the last's output. Handoffs without concurrency — the worst cost/reliability trade. Stages are named and ordered. Usually wants one agent instead.
Hierarchical supervisor (default) Control returns; one place plans, budgets and merges. The supervisor reads every result — it becomes the context bottleneck. Parallel subtasks under one objective.
Handoff / swarm The next agent owns the remainder; control doesn't return. No central merge, so no one place knows the whole state. Distinct domains: triage hands to billing, billing finishes.
Network / group chat Exploratory prototyping of interaction patterns. Every agent reads every turn; cost is agents × turns. You're testing whether agents disagreeing helps at all.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Sequential A chain with a contract per boundary. Sum of stages; no parallel saving. Failures name a stage; context loss at each handoff.
Supervisor Orchestrator, worker pool, merge node, per-worker budgets. Bounded by N × S; latency is the slowest worker. Supervisor context growth is the scaling limit.
Handoff / swarm Transfer primitives; state travels with the handoff. No merge cost, but no global view either. "Who has it now?" becomes a real operational question.
Group chat A shared transcript every agent reads. Grows with agents × turns — the worst profile of the four. Termination is the hard part: when does the conversation stop?

The redraw test: a supervisor has arrows out and back with a merge node; a swarm has arrows that only go forward. If your diagram's arrows all point onward and there's still a merge box, the topology and the picture disagree.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The agents kept talking to each other and the run only ended when it hit the wall-clock limit."

Root cause. A group-chat topology with four agents and a termination condition of "when the group agrees the task is complete". Agreement is not a property any single agent could assert, so each turn produced a plausible reason to continue — a refinement, a clarification, a suggestion someone should check something. Every turn was also read by all four agents, so cost grew with the square of the conversation length while the answer stopped improving after the third exchange.

Fix. A supervisor topology with a fixed worker set and an explicit merge, so termination became structural — workers return, the supervisor merges, the run ends. The lesson generalises past group chat: a topology where no single component owns termination will not terminate, and "they'll agree when it's done" is not a termination condition.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Orchestration Topologies — the shapes themselves.

  • Orchestrator-Worker Pattern — the default, in full.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §6 Delegation contract — a supervisor needs one; a swarm needs a handoff payload instead.

  • §5 Shared state across agents — swarms tempt you toward a blackboard, with the races that implies.

  • §3 Graph or free loop — a supervisor is usually a graph; a swarm usually isn't.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — hierarchical supervisor is the canonical answer.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — triage-then-handoff is the one place swarm shapes fit well.

notes.title: Which coordination failure you design against first

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Coordination problems observed in a production multi-agent system — How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

  • Durable execution — what makes a stuck or crashed worker recoverable — LangGraph: durable execution

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Coordination Problems — the failure taxonomy.

  • When Multi-Agent Hurts — the cases where these dominate.

What this note adds: the ordering and the fact that three of the four are prevented at dispatch rather than detected at runtime — so the design work happens in the orchestrator's planning step, not in monitoring.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four? Duplicated work · conflicting writes · context lost at handoff · workers that never finish.
Which are prevented at dispatch? Duplication, conflicts, and never-finishing — via the delegation contract.
Which can only be detected? Context loss at handoff — you find it in the output, not the trace.
Why duplication is worst? It's invisible: the answer looks well-supported and is redundant.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Three of the four coordination failures are prevented in the orchestrator's planning step rather than caught at runtime. Duplicated work is prevented by disjoint objectives, conflicting writes by serialising writes per resource or assigning ownership, and never-finishing workers by effort budgets with timeouts and defaults. The fourth — context lost at a handoff — can't be prevented by dispatch discipline, because you only discover what the summary dropped when something downstream needed it. So I design the first three out and instrument the fourth, which means keeping provenance on every finding that crosses a boundary.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Failure Prevent it by What it costs How you'd notice
Duplicated work Disjoint objectives assigned before dispatch, with explicit non-goals. More planning tokens per run. Overlap in sources touched; a confident, redundant answer.
Conflicting writes Serialise writes per resource, or give each worker an owned partition. Some serialisation latency on the write path. Last-write-wins losses; nothing errors.
Workers that never finish Effort budget, timeout, and a default on expiry. Coverage capped at the budget. One worker's cost dominating the run.
Context lost at handoff Can't prevent — carry provenance and make the gap visible. Larger payloads across boundaries. Downstream can't justify a claim it inherited.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you address Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Duplication The planner emits exclusions alongside objectives. Planning cost up, worker waste down — usually net cheaper. Overlap rate becomes a measurable planning-quality signal.
Conflicting writes A serialisation point or an ownership map per resource. Write-path latency. Contention is visible; silent overwrites stop.
Never-finishing Budgets in the contract, plus a watchdog and expiry default. Bounded worst case per worker. Budget-exhaustion rate tells you the decomposition is wrong.
Context loss Provenance fields on every cross-boundary payload. Larger handoff payloads. You can trace a claim back to its source, or find that you can't.

The redraw test: preventing the first three shows up in the orchestrator, not in new components — a planning node that outputs assignments, exclusions and budgets. If the diagram's orchestrator just fans out, none of this exists yet.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The report cited a source that doesn't say what the report claims it says."

Root cause. A worker found a document, drew a defensible conclusion in context, and returned a summary naming the document but not the passage or the reasoning. The supervisor merged summaries into a report and attached the citation. Downstream, the claim and the source had drifted apart — the worker's inference was reasonable given what it had read, but the merged sentence stated it more strongly, and nothing carried the intermediate step. No component was wrong in isolation, which is what made it hard to find.

Fix. Findings crossing a boundary carry provenance: the source id, the passage, and the worker's confidence. The merge can then check that a claim is supported by the passage rather than by the summary of it. This is the failure you instrument rather than prevent, and provenance is what makes the instrumentation possible at all.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Coordination Problems — the taxonomy this note orders.

  • Agent Communication — what a handoff payload can carry.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §6 Delegation contract — the contract's four fields are the prevention mechanism.

  • §5 Shared state across agents — conflicting writes are that decision's failure mode.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — worker write conflicts are the read/write split at agent scale.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — duplication and citation drift are its two characteristic failures.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — cross-team handoffs are where context loss is hardest to fix.

notes.title: Debate ensembles for quality
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Multiagent debate as a quality mechanism, and its cost profile — Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate (arXiv 2305.14325)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Debate and Critique Patterns — how debate and critique ensembles work.

What this note adds: where it sits — quality bought with disagreement at N× cost, and the correlation problem that decides whether the disagreement is real.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What it buys? Quality through disagreement, at N× cost per round.
The condition? Errors must be independent. Same model, same prompt, same blind spots.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Debate improves factuality by making several agents argue toward a position, and the research supports it. In production it's rarely the right spend: the cost is N agents times R rounds, and the benefit depends on the agents making independent errors. Run the same model with the same prompt N times and you get correlated confidence rather than genuine disagreement. If I wanted the effect cheaply, I'd diversify deliberately — different models or genuinely different framings — and cap it at two rounds, because that's where most of the gain lands.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No ensemble The default. A verifier is cheaper and stronger. Single-model blind spots. A deterministic check exists.
Diverse debate High-stakes judgement, no verifier, budget available. N × R model calls per answer. Different models available and the answer is worth it.
Same-model debate Rarely — the errors correlate. Full cost, much less benefit. "Run it three times and compare."
Verifier instead Anything with a checkable answer. One check per attempt. Tests, schema, execution, citation resolution.
